title: A whole surah opens on a short scale.
subtitle: Why small cheating gets a loud warning
then: The traders of Makkah lived by the scale and the measuring cup. Ibn Kathir reports that when the Prophet ﷺ reached Madinah, people there were known for cheating on measure. {idea}This surah was recited, and they began to give full measure.{/idea}
now: The invoice rounded up by fifteen minutes. The used phone sold with the cracked corner hidden in the photos. The extra item you let slide at the self-checkout. {trap}Small enough that nobody checks.{/trap}
old: A little off the top is just how business works.
new: The small cut is exactly what Allah chose to open a surah with.
try: Check one bill, timesheet or sale you made this week. Make sure the other person got their full due.

title: When they receive, they want every last grain.
subtitle: The first half of a double standard

row.title: I just want what is fair

then: Ibn Kathir explains that these people took their right in full and pressed for extra when buying from others. {trap}They knew exactly what a full measure looked like{/trap}, because they insisted on it for themselves.
now: You count the change from the cashier twice. You chase the refund to the last cent. You notice the moment a colleague takes credit for your idea. {idea}You already know what fairness feels like from the receiving end.{/idea}
old: Making sure I get my full share is just being careful.
new: How I measure for myself shows that I know the standard I owe others.
try: Notice one place today where you insist on your full share. Ask if you give the same to others.

title: When they give, the scale quietly shrinks.
subtitle: The second half of the double standard

row.title: two measures
sub: one for me, one for you

then: Measuring by volume or weighing by scale, they made others lose. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah commands full weight elsewhere, and that {trap}the people of Shu'ayb were destroyed for this same cheating{/trap}.
now: You want your manager to pay overtime to the minute, but your own lunch break stretches. You want the landlord to fix things fast, but your rent is late. {idea}Two rulers in one pocket.{/idea}
old: Everyone shaves a bit off when they are the one paying.
new: Giving less than I would accept is the very thing this verse names.
try: Give one person today a little more than their due: time, effort or money.

title: Cheating starts where the thought of rising again stops.
subtitle: The root behind the short scale
then: The surah introduction explains that this one evil is given as an example of what happens when people forget the Hereafter. {idea}Honesty that rests only on being watched breaks when no one is watching.{/idea} The verse asks: do they not even think about it?
now: Working from home with no one checking your screen. The expense form nobody audits. The exam where the invigilator steps out. {trap}The test is not the rule. It is who you think is looking.{/trap}
old: If no one will ever find out, it does not really count.
new: Someone will raise me and ask, and that changes the private moments.
try: In one unwatched moment today, do the honest thing and remind yourself why.

title: Small profit, set against a tremendous Day.
subtitle: Putting the gain on the right scale
then: Ibn Kathir describes the Day as one of great horror and tremendous fright, before the One who knows hidden secrets. {idea}The verse makes the cheater's small gain look its real size.{/idea}
now: You lie awake over a fifty-dollar dispute with a seller. The anger at a colleague over a parking spot. {reward}Put it next to the Great Day and most of it shrinks.{/reward}
old: This little advantage is worth fighting for.
new: Next to the Great Day, what I am grabbing is almost nothing.
try: Pick one petty gain you are chasing and let it go today.

title: Everyone stands, and the Lord of all is before them.
subtitle: The standing that ends every deal
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that people will stand until some sink in sweat to the middle of their ears, each according to their deeds. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge from the hardship of that standing{/idea} in his night prayer.
now: You stand in a long queue at the bank and feel your patience thin. You wait in a hospital corridor for news. {reward}Standing makes you honest about what you have and have not done.{/reward}
old: I answer to my boss, my clients, maybe the tax office.
new: In the end I stand before the Lord of everything, and so does everyone I dealt with.
try: In your next prayer, ask Allah to make the standing easy for you, as the Prophet ﷺ did.

title: No. The record of the wicked is kept in Sijjin.
subtitle: Where a cheating life is filed
then: The verse opens with a sharp No, cutting off the idea that no reckoning comes. Ibn Kathir says Sijjin is taken from the word for prison and means {trap}straitened, narrow circumstances{/trap}, the final abode of the wicked.
now: Every app keeps a history: your search log, your messages, your bank statements. {idea}You already live in a world where nothing is truly deleted.{/idea} The verse says your deeds have a record too.
old: Once it is done and forgotten, it is gone.
new: What I do is filed somewhere, and the file has a destination.
try: Tonight, think of one thing you would not want in your record. Ask Allah's forgiveness for it.

title: And what will make you know what Sijjin is?
subtitle: A question that makes it heavier
then: Ibn Kathir says this question expresses how great the matter is: {trap}an eternal prison and a painful torment{/trap}. The listeners in Makkah were stopped mid-sentence and made to wonder.
now: A doctor says, "Sit down, we need to talk." You know before the words come that it is serious. {idea}The question works the same way. It makes you sit down.{/idea}
old: I already know roughly what the warnings say.
new: Allah's question tells me this is bigger than I have pictured.
try: When you hear a warning in the Quran today, stop for one breath before moving on.

title: A register inscribed. Nothing added, nothing erased.
subtitle: The record is closed and complete
then: Ibn Kathir, citing Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi, explains that the destination is {trap}inscribed, written, and completed. No one can add to it and no one can remove from it.{/trap}
now: The email you cannot unsend. The exam paper already handed in. The contract signed and filed. {reward}Right now your page is still open, and repentance still writes on it.{/reward}
old: There will always be time to fix my record.
new: One day the register closes. Today it is still open.
try: Do one thing today you would want written in your record: a call, a charity, an apology.

title: Woe that Day to those who called it a lie.
subtitle: The second woe of the surah
then: The surah began with woe to those who cheat. Now it ties a second woe to those who deny. Ibn Kathir says woe means {trap}destruction and devastation{/trap} when they come to their imprisonment.
now: You may never say "I deny the Day" out loud. But the way you split a bill or fill a timesheet speaks too. {idea}Denial can live in habits, not only in words.{/idea}
old: I believe in the Day, so this warning is not about me.
new: My daily dealings show how much I really believe the Day is coming.
try: Pick one habit that acts as if no Day is coming. Change it a little today.

title: They deny the Day when everything is repaid.
subtitle: What exactly they refused to believe
then: Ibn Kathir explains that they did not believe the Day would happen and {trap}considered it far-fetched{/trap}. In early Makkah, surah after surah was revealed to set this belief in people's hearts.
now: Someone wrongs you and gets away with it. A kindness you did goes unthanked for years. {reward}The Day of Recompense means neither is lost.{/reward}
old: Some things in life just never get settled.
new: There is a Day set aside to repay everything, the good I did included.
try: Think of one unthanked good deed you did. Leave its reward with Allah and feel lighter.

title: Only the one who keeps crossing lines denies it.
subtitle: Denial and wrongdoing feed each other

row.title: conduct shapes belief
sub: what I do bends what I accept

then: Ibn Kathir describes this person as {trap}transgressive in deeds and sinful in speech{/trap}: he lies when he speaks, breaks promises, and is abusive when he argues. Denying the Day lets him carry on.
now: Once you have padded one expense claim, the next is easier, and the rules start to feel silly. {idea}Behaviour quietly writes your beliefs for you.{/idea} Keeping small promises keeps the heart honest.
old: My doubts come from thinking, not from how I live.
new: The lines I keep crossing can make the truth harder for me to accept.
try: Keep one small promise today exactly as you made it.

title: Hearing the verses, he says: old stories.
subtitle: Dismissing what you do not want to face
then: Ibn Kathir says whenever this man heard Allah's words from the Messenger ﷺ, he {trap}denied them and thought ill of them{/trap}, claiming they were gathered from the books of earlier peoples. The same line appears in other surahs.
now: A reminder comes up in the family group chat and you scroll past: "heard it before." A talk at the masjid feels old-fashioned. {idea}Calling something old is an easy way to never let it reach you.{/idea}
old: I have heard all this before. It is nothing new.
new: A verse I know by heart can still be speaking to me today.
try: Read one short verse you know well, slowly, as if hearing it for the first time.

title: No. What they earned has rusted over their hearts.
subtitle: Why truth stopped getting through
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith from Abu Hurayrah: when a servant sins, a black spot appears in his heart. {reward}If he repents, his heart is polished clean.{/reward} {trap}If he returns, it grows until it covers the heart.{/trap}
now: A phone screen with years of fingerprints. You do not notice the smudge until you hold it to the light. {idea}One honest istighfar wipes a spot before it hardens.{/idea}
old: One more slip will not change anything about me.
new: Each sin leaves a mark, and each repentance can wipe one clean.
try: Before sleeping tonight, say astaghfirullah slowly for one specific thing.

title: That Day, they are screened from their Lord.
subtitle: The loss beneath every other loss
then: Right after the covered heart comes the veil. Ibn Kathir reports Imam Ash-Shafi'i saying that {reward}this verse is proof that the believers will see Allah on that Day{/reward}, since only the deniers are screened.
now: You sit in the same room as someone you love but are both on your phones. Close, yet shut out. {idea}What you let cover your heart now shapes what you will see later.{/idea}
old: The worst thing about the Hereafter would be the pain.
new: The deepest loss is being kept from seeing my Lord.
try: Ask Allah today, in your own words, to let you see Him on that Day.

title: Then they enter the Fire they denied.
subtitle: The end of the denier's road
then: The surah lays out the steps plainly: a sealed record, a covered heart, a veil, and {trap}then the Fire{/trap}. It was spoken to Makkans who were laughing at the warning while there was still time.
now: A sat-nav keeps saying "turn around when possible." You can ignore it for miles, but each exit is a chance. {reward}Every day you are alive is an exit off this road.{/reward}
old: Warnings about the Fire are for other kinds of people.
new: The warning is a mercy because it comes while I can still turn.
try: Name one thing you keep putting off changing. Take the first small step today.

title: This is what you used to call a lie.
subtitle: The moment denial meets the fact
then: The same people who said {trap}legends of the former peoples{/trap} in verse 13 now hear it turned back: this is the very thing you denied. The surah closes the loop on their own words.
now: The warning light on the car dashboard you kept ignoring, until the breakdown. The doctor's advice you laughed off, until the test results. {idea}Better to believe the warning before it becomes the event.{/idea}
old: I will take it seriously if it ever actually happens.
new: By the time it happens, it is too late to start believing it.
try: Act on one reminder today that you have been brushing off.

title: No. The record of the righteous rises to Illiyyin.
subtitle: The opposite file, the opposite place
then: Ibn Kathir says the righteous are in the opposite situation to the wicked. Illiyyin is taken from the word for {reward}highness{/reward}. Ibn Abbas said it means Paradise; others placed it in the seventh heaven.
now: The quiet charity, the night you held your tongue, the parent you visited after a long shift. {reward}None of it vanished. It went up.{/reward}
old: My small good deeds probably do not add up to much.
new: The good I do is filed in a high place, and it keeps rising.
try: Do one hidden good deed today that only Allah will know about.

title: And what will make you know what Illiyyin is?
subtitle: The same question, now about honour
then: The same question that made Sijjin heavy now makes Illiyyin grand. Ibn Kathir says {reward}Allah magnifies its affair and extols its matter{/reward} by asking it.
now: You picture the dream job or the dream house and it is already small next to the real thing. {idea}What Allah has prepared is bigger than any picture you can hold.{/idea}
old: I have a rough idea of what reward looks like.
new: The reward is greater than anything I can picture, so it is worth reaching for.
try: Spend one minute today imagining the best of Paradise, then thank Allah for the hope.

title: Their place too is written in a sealed register.
subtitle: Good deeds are recorded just as firmly
then: The exact phrase from verse 9 returns, "a register inscribed." Ibn Kathir says it affirms {reward}what will be written for the righteous{/reward}. The firmness that warned the wicked now comforts the good.
now: Your boss forgot the extra project you did. Your kids will not remember the nights you stayed up. {reward}The register does not forget.{/reward}
old: If nobody saw it, it might as well not have happened.
new: Every good deed is written firmly, whether or not anyone noticed.
try: Recall one good thing you did that no one thanked you for. Let that be enough.

title: Those brought near bear witness to it.
subtitle: An honoured record with honoured witnesses
then: Qatadah said those brought near are the angels. Ibn Abbas said {reward}those nearest to Allah in each heaven will witness it{/reward}. The record of the righteous is seen and honoured.
now: You hold back from posting the volunteer photo and feel a small sting nobody saw it. {idea}Someone did. A better audience than any feed.{/idea}
old: Good deeds feel wasted if no one sees them.
new: My good is witnessed by those near to Allah, which is better than any audience here.
try: Do one good deed today and tell no one about it.

title: The righteous will be in delight.
subtitle: Where the honest scale finally leads
then: Ibn Kathir says the righteous will be in {reward}eternal pleasure and gardens of comprehensive bounties{/reward}. It answers the cheaters at the start of the surah: honesty is not a loss.
now: You turned down the side deal that would have paid for a holiday. You told the customer about the defect. {reward}It felt like losing at the time.{/reward} The verse says it was not.
old: Being honest in business means I will always earn less.
new: Honesty leads to a delight that no shortcut can buy.
try: Next time honesty costs you a little today, say alhamdulillah and keep going.

title: On raised couches, they look.
subtitle: At rest, and given sight
then: Ibn Kathir gives two meanings: they look at the kingdom and bounties Allah gave them, or {reward}they look at Allah, the Mighty and Sublime{/reward}. Either way it is the opposite of the veil in verse 15.
now: After a long week you finally sit down and just look out the window, no rush. {reward}Imagine that rest, but forever, and with the best view there is.{/reward}
old: Rest is something I will never really get.
new: A rest is coming where I sit at ease and see what matters most.
try: Take five quiet minutes today to sit, look at something Allah made, and say subhanAllah.

title: You will see the glow of delight on their faces.
subtitle: Joy that shows from the inside
then: Ibn Kathir says you will notice a {reward}glow of delight in their faces{/reward}, a sign of happiness, composure and honour from the great bounty they are in.
now: You can tell when someone is truly happy: a grandparent holding a new baby, a friend just out of hospital. {reward}No filter needed.{/reward} That is the kind of face this verse describes.
old: Happiness is something you show, even if you do not feel it.
new: Real delight shines out without trying.
try: Smile at one person today and mean it.

title: They are given a pure, sealed drink.
subtitle: A drink kept closed until it reaches them
then: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said Rahiq is one of the names of {reward}the drink of Paradise{/reward}. It is sealed, kept intact for those it was meant for.
now: The thrill of breaking the seal on something new that is truly yours. A gift box wrapped just for you. {reward}Paradise keeps its best things sealed for their owners.{/reward}
old: The good things are always taken before I get there.
new: What Allah has kept for me is sealed and waiting.
try: Give someone a small gift today, wrapped with care, and think of what Allah has wrapped for you.

title: Its last note is musk. Compete for this.
subtitle: The one race worth running
then: Ibn Abbas said Allah makes the last thing placed in it musk. Then the verse says: for this let the competitors compete. Ibn Kathir links it to {idea}"for the like of this let the workers work."{/idea} The surah began with men competing over grams.
now: You check a colleague's salary, a friend's new car, a cousin's holiday photos. {trap}Competing is natural.{/trap} {idea}The verse just points it at a better finish line.{/idea}
old: Competing with others is unhealthy and I should feel guilty about it.
new: Competing is fine. The question is what I am racing for.
try: Pick one good deed and try to beat yesterday's version of yourself at it today.

title: It is blended from Tasnim, the highest spring.
subtitle: Even the drink has ranks
then: Abu Salih and Ad-Dahhak said Tasnim is {reward}the most excellent and exalted drink of the people of Paradise{/reward}. The righteous are given a drink mixed with it.
now: You are happy with a good grade, then hear there is a distinction above it. {idea}Not envy, just a reason to reach a little higher.{/idea}
old: Just getting in is enough. I do not need to aim higher.
new: Paradise has ranks, and I am allowed to hope for the highest.
try: Add one extra voluntary act today: two rakahs, a page of Quran, or a small charity.

title: A spring the near ones drink from directly.
subtitle: The closer you are, the purer the drink
then: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Masruq and Qatadah said those brought near will drink from Tasnim pure as they wish, while {reward}the companions of the right hand are given it mixed{/reward}.
now: At work the front-row seats go to whoever knows the boss. {idea}Here, nearness is not bought or networked.{/idea} It is built one prayer, one kindness at a time.
old: Closeness to Allah is for special people, not someone like me.
new: Nearness is earned by what I do, and the door is open to me.
try: Do one act today purely to be closer to Allah, with no other reason.

title: The guilty used to laugh at those who believed.
subtitle: Ridicule as the first weapon
then: The surah introduction says it came when Makkans had started {trap}ridiculing the Muslims in streets and assemblies{/trap}, before open persecution began. Ibn Kathir says they mocked and despised the believers.
now: You pray at work and a colleague jokes about it. A relative teases you for not drinking at the party. {idea}It stings, but laughter has never been an argument.{/idea} And check that you are never the one laughing at someone's sincerity.
old: If people laugh at what I do, maybe I am doing it wrong.
new: Being mocked for doing right says nothing about whether it is right.
try: Next time someone mocks a good habit of yours, answer kindly and keep the habit.

title: As they passed, they winked at each other.
subtitle: Contempt in a glance
then: Ibn Kathir says whenever they passed by the believers, {trap}they would wink at each other in contempt{/trap}. No words, no blows, just a shared look. Allah still put it in the Quran.
now: The eye-roll across the office when the new hire speaks. The side glance with a friend when someone in hijab walks in. {trap}A look can be a whole sentence.{/trap}
old: A look is harmless. I never said anything.
new: Even a mocking glance is a deed that gets written.
try: Catch one eye-roll or smirk before it happens today. Replace it with a neutral face.

title: They went home pleased, joking about it.
subtitle: Comfort without gratitude
then: Ibn Kathir says they returned to their families pleased, finding whatever they wanted. {trap}Yet they were not grateful for Allah's favour{/trap} and busied themselves with despising and envying the believers.
now: Dinner at home, plenty on the table, and the conversation turns to mocking someone from work or school. {idea}The verse asks what you do with your comfort.{/idea}
old: Joking about people at home is just harmless venting.
new: Comfort is a blessing to thank Allah for, not a stage for mocking others.
try: At your next family meal, steer one conversation from mockery to gratitude.

title: Seeing them, they said: these people are lost.
subtitle: The verdict passed by the mockers
then: Ibn Kathir says they called the believers misguided {trap}because they followed a religion other than their own{/trap}. Later in the surah he notes they were not misguided at all but close friends of Allah.
now: Your choice to quit a dodgy job, or marry simply, or pray on time gets called naive by people who are sure they know better. {idea}Their certainty is not proof.{/idea}
old: If everyone around me thinks I am lost, maybe I am.
new: Other people's verdict on me is not Allah's verdict.
try: Write down one good choice you made that others questioned. Thank Allah for it.

title: Nobody appointed them guardians over the believers.
subtitle: Minding someone else's record
then: Ibn Kathir says these people were not made responsible for the believers' deeds or words. {idea}So why were they so concerned with them, making them the focus of their attention?{/idea}
now: You know exactly what your cousin does wrong, what your neighbour wears, who in the group chat skipped Ramadan fasts. {trap}You were not sent as their guard.{/trap} {idea}Your own record needs the time.{/idea}
old: Someone has to keep an eye on what others are doing.
new: I am not anyone's guardian. My own deeds are my job.
try: Next time you start judging someone today, switch to one question about yourself instead.

title: Today the believers are the ones who laugh.
subtitle: The laughter changes sides
then: Ibn Kathir says this is on the Day of Judgement, {reward}as recompense for how they were laughed at{/reward}. He links it to another passage where Allah rewards a party of His servants for their patience.
now: The years you spent being the odd one out for your faith at school or work. {reward}They are not wasted. They are part of what turns into joy.{/reward}
old: Being mocked for my faith is just something I have to swallow.
new: Patience with mockery turns into joy that will not end.
try: Make a short dua today for patience with anyone who makes fun of your faith.

title: From raised couches, they look on.
subtitle: The same scene, now as reward for patience
then: Verse 23 is repeated, but here Ibn Kathir ties it to the mockery: they look at Allah {reward}as reward for bearing the false claims that they were misguided{/reward}.
now: You were the one walked past and whispered about. {reward}This verse pictures you seated, calm, and looking at the One you stayed true to.{/reward}
old: Standing firm while being mocked gets me nothing.
new: Every whisper I bore patiently is building toward that seat.
try: Stay calm the next time someone belittles you today. Picture this seat.

title: Have they not been paid for what they did?
subtitle: The scale the surah began with, balanced
then: Ibn Kathir explains the question means they surely {idea}will be paid in full, completely and perfectly{/idea}, for their mockery and contempt. The surah that began with short measure ends with Allah's full measure.
now: Before you send that sarcastic reply, or pocket the extra change, remember that every deal is settled exactly. {reward}The same exactness means your good is repaid in full too.{/reward}
old: Some people get away with it, and that is just life.
new: Allah gives everyone full measure, the measure I give included.
try: Settle one small debt or wrong today before it waits for that Day.
